signals.title: Nvidia releases Dynamo recipes for four South Korean open models
signals.excerpt:
Nvidia released Dynamo deployment recipes for four South Korean open models on 8 November, saying the B200-optimised software delivers up to 2x performance for inference across multiple GPUs, according to a company blog post announcing the release.

## Key points

- The recipes cover models from SK Telecom, LG AI Research, Upstage and Motif Technologies.
- Nvidia says Dynamo coordinates requests and communication when inference runs across multiple GPUs.
- LG AI Research is reviewing Dynamo for its own model operations.
- LG is separately making a newer K-EXAONE model available through a free API.

...

The release covers A.X K2 from SK Telecom, K-EXAONE 2.0 from LG AI Research, Solar Open 2 from Upstage and Motif-3 from Motif Technologies. Nvidia describes Dynamo as an open-source framework for serving AI models across multiple machines in a data centre. The recipes are optimised for its B200 GPUs.

A model too large for one GPU has to run across several, Nvidia says. That requires the serving system to direct incoming requests and coordinate communication between GPUs. Dynamo handles those tasks across multiple machines, according to the company. The recipes provide deployment configurations for the four named models rather than new versions of the models themselves.

Nvidia says the configurations deliver up to 2x performance out of the box and can help developers move the models into production faster. The claim concerns inference serving: running a trained model to generate responses. It is separate from claims about a model’s ability to complete a task. Nvidia positions the recipes for deployments in which a single GPU cannot hold the model.

...

LG AI Research says K-EXAONE 2.5 performed more than 70 percent better than the model released in August on a combined assessment of 24 evaluation metrics. That is LG’s assessment of model performance, rather than Nvidia’s claim about the speed of the Dynamo deployment recipes.

In LG’s internal evaluation using public datasets, K-EXAONE 2.5 scored 74.6 on AutomationBench, which tests work automation using software services. LG put DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at 74.9 and GLM 5.3 Max at 71.6 on the same measure. The company also reported scores of 78.0 on BrowseComp, a web-browsing test, and 59.2 on SWE-Bench Pro, a software-development test.

signals.title: Introducing AgentEnv: An Open-Source Framework for Building RL Environments | Scale Labs
signals.excerpt:
10/5/2026

# Introducing AgentEnv: An Open-Source Framework for Building RL Environments

By Edgar Arakelyan, Tejas Polakam, Yzabelle Go

An agent is only as good as the world it operates in, and building worlds that are realistic, accurate, and scalable all at once is the hard part of scaling RL. Every RL environment Scale builds runs on AgentEnv. Today we're open-sourcing it.

...

Most tools for agent training start from the task and build a world around it. AgentEnv’s philosophy starts from the world first, so one Environment can host many Tasks and many agents. AgentEnv is built on two core principles

Building blocks: What an Environment is made of. An Environment is built from versioned composable blocks: Environments like Slack or Gmail, an Artifact of data that populates them, and Rules (the clock, triggers, and roles) that govern how it behaves.

Interoperability: What an Environment works with. An Environment doesn't assume anything about who or what runs it. Any agent can connect to it, any sandbox can host it, and your cloud can run it, all through open protocols instead of custom glue.

...

#### Designed for Interoperability

Agent Agnostic. An Environment's card tells an agent which tools it serves and how to reach them, over MCP, REST or a generated CLI. An agent's Agent Card, from the open A2A protocol, does the same in the other direction.

Pair any Environment Card with any Agent Card and the agent can start work, with no custom wiring. The same Task runs unchanged and consistent on Claude Code, OpenAI's agents, or any of your own custom agents.

...

A Task is constructed as a DAG of AgentEnv steps. Each step represents a primitive action on an Agent, the Environment and more, like setting up the world, loading data, setting the clock, bringing in an agent, handing it the work, collecting what it made, grading the result with a rubric or a strict check.

...

### What comes out of the box

AgentEnv ships 48 built-in step types, covering everything from deploying an Environment to setting its Rules of the World to grading trajectories. Most RL Tasks can be built from these alone, with no new code. For the rest, you can add your own steps as plugins.

signals.title: CMU Researchers Release ServerBench to Test AI-Driven LLM Serving Systems | Automatica Press
signals.excerpt:
CMU's ServerBench evaluates coding agents on designing LLM serving systems under real workloads, with Claude Sonnet 5.5 achieving 4.87x the vLLM baseline on Gemma E4B but only 22 of 33 agent-built systems passing validation.

...

R esearchers at Carnegie Mellon University and the University of Southern California released ServerBench, a benchmark that evaluates coding agents' ability to design large language model serving systems, in a preprint on arXiv this month.

ServerBench assesses agents on a 'dollars per dollar' objective — latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost — under real workload conditions, according to the paper ServerBench paper 1. The benchmark requires agents to build a complete serving system from a minimal starter, making decisions about the scheduler, KV cache, batching, kernels, and the number of concurrent sessions. Stateful replay preserves session dependencies from recorded coding-agent sessions, and an independent verification step checks that the submitted system meets latency targets and produces correct outputs.

...

Across 11 coding-agent models and three model-hardware deployments on L40 GPUs, Claude Sonnet 5.5 achieved 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, or 4.87 times the vLLM baseline, according to the paper. The GitHub repository lists the deployments and results: Gemma E4B on a single L40 GPU reached 4.87 times the strongest baseline (vLLM at 0.61 dollars per dollar), Qwen3.5 9B on two L40 GPUs reached 2.72 times the strongest baseline (SGLang at 1.62 dollars per dollar), and Qwen3.8 27B INT4 on two L40 GPUs reached 1.80 times the strongest baseline (vLLM at 1.47 dollars per dollar) GitHub repository 3. Of 33 total runs, 22 yielded systems that passed verification.

The scoring mechanism includes a latency gate: only requests that meet both time-to-first-token and time-per-output-token targets count toward the score. The system is rebuilt fresh, replayed on held-out seeds, and checked for prompt completeness, output lengths, streaming consistency, fidelity to the checkpoint, and answer accuracy; only verified systems receive a score, the paper states ServerBench paper 2.

The paper is a preprint with no stated peer review or independent replication. All results are the authors' own, run on their own harness. The benchmark conditions include an 8-hour development budget per run, with agents running through Claude Code or Codex, and a 1,800-second final replay on a held-out workload seed.

signals.title: NVIDIA Auto Ontology: Graph-Based Semantic Layer for AI | AIToolly
signals.excerpt:
# NVIDIA Introduces Auto Ontology: A Python Framework for Graph-Based Semantic Reasoning in LLM Workflows

NVIDIA has released Auto Ontology, an open-source Python framework designed to establish a graph-based semantic reasoning layer over data. Built to address common challenges in modern artificial intelligence deployments, the framework facilitates deterministic query generation, superior context retrieval, and enhanced explainability for large language models (LLMs) and autonomous AI agent workflows. By structuring data semantics into an interconnected knowledge graph representation, Auto Ontology bridges the gap between raw data stores and generative language architectures, ensuring agentic systems query underlying information accurately and interpret context reliably.

November 7, 2026 at 06:45 AM GitHub Trending Share

...

- Graph-Based Semantic Layer: NVIDIA's Auto Ontology provides a dedicated Python framework to build graph-based semantic reasoning layers directly over existing data architectures.
- Deterministic Query Generation: The framework enables large language models (LLMs) and agent workflows to generate precise, deterministic queries instead of relying entirely on speculative or probabilistic generation.
- Superior Context Retrieval: By organizing semantic structures into graph representations, the framework significantly optimizes how relevant context is discovered and fed into generative models.
- Explainable Artificial Intelligence: Auto Ontology enhances transparency across AI workflows, giving developers verifiable and interpretable paths for how queries and agent decisions are formed.

...

### Deterministic Query Generation for LLM and Agent Systems

One of the core capabilities delivered by Auto Ontology is deterministic query generation. Traditional LLM-driven query synthesis—such as direct text-to-SQL or ad-hoc API generation—frequently introduces non-deterministic outputs where the same natural language prompt may yield different query structures, syntactic errors, or incorrect joins across runs.

By anchoring language models and agent workflows to a defined semantic graph, Auto Ontology transforms query generation into a constrained, deterministic operation. The semantic relationships defined within the ontology dictate the valid traversals, schemas, and relational constraints available to the model. As autonomous AI agents execute multi-step workflows, deterministic query generation guarantees that every synthesized query corresponds to valid schema definitions and authentic data relationships, drastically reducing runtime failures and data retrieval errors.

### Enhancing Context Retrieval and Advancing Explainable AI

Context retrieval is central to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agentic reasoning architectures. Standard vector-based similarity retrieval often retrieves text fragments that share surface-level linguistic commonality but lack semantic cohesion or relational depth. In contrast, Auto Ontology optimizes context retrieval by leveraging graph structures that capture deep, multi-hop semantic connections.

...

Auto Ontology is an open-source Python framework developed by NVIDIA that builds a graph-based semantic reasoning layer on top of data, specifically created to support large language models (LLMs) and autonomous AI agent workflows.

signals.title: Buoyant Releases Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for Kubernetes and vLLM - MarkTechPost
signals.excerpt:
Michal Sutter

November 7, 2026

Buoyant, the company behind Linkerd, has released Kinference, an open source project for building inference platforms on Kubernetes. Kinference is an inference control plane for Kubernetes and vLLM. It sits in front of a fleet of vLLM workers and decides where each request goes. It applies routing policies, token rate limits, KV-cache-aware load balancing and per-tenant metrics in one layer. For dev teams serving many open-weight models to many internal clients, it targets the layer above the model server. The project is Apache 2.0 licensed on GitHub. The current release is v0.1.0-alpha.7.

## TL;DR

- Size: v0.1.0-alpha.7, written in Rust, Apache 2.0, configured through 5 Kubernetes CRDs.
- Runs on: any GPU-enabled Kubernetes cluster running vLLM. Buoyant’s benchmark used 3 L40S GPUs per pool.
- Performance: large gains on prefix-heavy traffic versus plain Kubernetes Service routing (self-reported).
- Best: median TTFT fell from 6.88 s to 0.31 s (95%) on a shared-prefix workload.
- Worst: no median TTFT gain on prompts without shared prefixes (6.92 s vs 6.83 s).

...

## How fast is Kinference in benchmarks?

Buoyant published a benchmark against plain Kubernetes load balancing. Each arm used 3 vLLM 0.31.0 pods, each on 1 L40S GPU. The model was Qwen3.8-27B-FP8. Load came from GuideLLM 0.8.1. The baseline was a ClusterIP Service, where kube-proxy picks a random pod per connection.

Unloaded latency results (median TTFT):

| Workload | Kubernetes Service | Kinference | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control (no shared prefix) | 6.92 s | 6.83 s | No significant difference |
| Shared-prefix | 6.88 s | 0.31 s | about -95% |
| Multiturn | 1.70 s | 0.59 s | about -65% |

Median end-to-end latency fell 45% on shared-prefix and 32% on multiturn. On control traffic, p95 TTFT still dropped from 21.46 s to 12.33 s. Buoyant attributes this to queue-aware balancing.

The capacity test measured goodput: requests per minute meeting a TTFT SLO. Peak goodput was 103.0 vs 14.0 req/min on shared-prefix, about 7.4x. On multiturn it was 82.7 vs 23.8, about 3.5x. The Service baseline never met the SLO at any tested concurrency.

signals.title: NVIDIA’s Open-Source Semantic Layer Makes Agents Verify Metrics First | opcnew
signals.excerpt:
# NVIDIA’s Open-Source Semantic Layer Makes Agents Verify Metrics First

## What this is

On November 5 and 6, NVIDIA’s open-source auto-ontology ranked first on GitHub’s Python trending list for two consecutive days, receiving about 2,000 Stars in a single day. What matters here is not “how to find data faster,” but “under what rules the numbers retrieved are actually calculated.”

In practice, “revenue” may mean the total including refunds or only paid orders. Text-to-SQL, which lets a model convert natural language into database queries, can produce a query but cannot access the business definitions scattered across documents, reports, and employees’ experience. auto-ontology therefore inserts a semantic layer between the database and the Agent: it organizes business terms, metric formulas, and table relationships into certifiable definitions that the Agent can invoke before generating a query.

Here, an “ontology” can be understood as a machine-readable enterprise dictionary. It includes business terminology and synonyms, reviewed SQL metric expressions, and join paths between tables. Retrieval still relies on vector similarity, but the final calculation rules come from human-approved versions. The project also supports integration with existing systems through MCP, the standard connection mechanism that lets Agents call external tools and data.

...

We believe this project addresses an underestimated bottleneck in enterprise AI deployment: a model’s ability to write SQL does not mean the business trusts its results. Maintaining a unified semantic layer requires greater upfront effort than assembling prompts on the fly or slicing documents and feeding them into RAG, which retrieves external material before passing it to the model for an answer. But it can provide more stable definitions, traceable calculations, and the ability to “refuse to answer when it cannot respond reliably.”

The objections are just as clear. A semantic layer does not automatically eliminate errors: business terms, metric formulas, and join relationships still require review by domain experts, and machines may not discover every implicit rule embedded in historical reports. The project’s official example generated only 31 terms from Microsoft’s Wide World Importers database. That demonstrates the workflow is feasible, but it does not show that the approach can cover the complex data assets of a large enterprise at low cost.

signals.excerpt:
# Speed Up Image Generation with FLUX 3 Image Klein on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs

 Nov 06, 2026 

 By Olivia Stoner, Yiheng Zhang, Chang Liu, Seonghee Lee and Gunjan Mehta

...

- FLUX 3 Image Klein Base and its distilled variant combine Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct for text conditioning, a diffusion transformer, and an autoencoder to generate and edit images at high resolution.
- TensorRT LLM VisualGen accelerates inference on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with NVFP4 quantization, fused PrimsTS GEMM kernels, and torch.compile, delivering up to 1.62x faster text-to-image and 1.58x faster image-to-image generation over BF16 on a single B200.
- Quantized attention options include cuDNN FP8 and VC-Attention FP8; VC-Attention FP8 with a repair budget of 0.005 achieved 1.18x speedups for both Base and distilled models at 2048x2048 with LPIPS scores of 0.086 and 0.151.
- Sol-Attention sparse attention with τ=1.0 and 12 initial dense steps provided 1.30x faster denoising plus decoding for Base, while 16 dense steps prioritized fidelity at 1.24x.
- Cache-DiT step caching nearly halved Base latency at both 1024x1024 and 2048x2048, reaching 1.94x speedup at the higher resolution with an LPIPS of 0.033.
- Multi-GPU scaling with CFG and Ulysses parallelism on eight B200 GPUs reduced median T2I latency from 14.90 to 3.00 seconds for Base and from 2.73 to 1.08 seconds for distilled, with denoising speedups of 6.01x and 4.44x.

...

FLUX 3 Image Klein is an image editing and generation model from Black Forest Labs (BFL) trained on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 and optimized for NVIDIA GPUs. It offers Base and distilled checkpoints for different latency and fidelity requirements.

This tutorial shows how to configure FLUX 3 Image Klein in NVIDIA TensorRT LLM VisualGen to take advantage of fused kernels, multi-GPU parallelism, FP8/NVFP4 support, caching, and attention optimizations. It compares latency and changes in generated outputs across optimizations. In the reported 2048×2048 tests on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU, combined optimizations delivered up to 3.46x faster text-to-image (T2I) and 4.45x faster image-to-image (I2I) generation for FLUX 3 Image Klein Base compared with uncompiled BF16 inference. The tutorial includes deployment instructions and YAML configurations for applying these optimizations to your workloads.

...

TensorRT LLM VisualGen, a dedicated runtime within TensorRT LLM, supported BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 variants at launch. On an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU, NVFP4 delivered up to 1.62x faster T2I and 1.58x faster I2I generation than BF16. Figure 2 compares generation latency, while Figure 1 compares example outputs. The following sections use NVFP4 as the starting point for further optimization.

...

...

TensorRT LLM VisualGen uses FlashInfer’s PrimsTS FP8/NVFP4 GEMM kernels, built with CUTLASS Primitives and Task Scheduling to accelerate quantized inference. Tuned for FLUX 3 tensor shapes and enabled by default, they combine optimized GEMMs with fused epilogues, including GEMM with SwiGLU and query, key, and value (QKV) projections with query/key normalization and rotary position embeddings (RoPE). See FlashInfer PR #5758 for more details.

...

Attention is a major bottleneck in high-resolution image generation. In the reported 2048×2048 NVFP4 T2I tests on B200, VANILLA BF16 attention accounted for approximately 60% of DiT GPU kernel time for both Base and distilled Klein. VisualGen supports two approaches to reducing this cost: quantized attention with cuDNN FP8 or VC-Attention FP8, and sparse attention with Sol-Attention. VC-Attention FP8 is a TensorRT LLM variant of the method described in the VC-Attention paper.

...

The VisualGen runtime in TensorRT LLM scales FLUX 3 Image Klein using classifier-free guidance (CFG) and Ulysses sequence parallelism. Base assigns positive/negative branches to separate GPU groups and partitions each branch’s sequence with Ulysses; distilled runs without CFG and uses Ulysses alone.

At 2048×2048, scaling from one to eight GPUs on an NVIDIA DGX B200 reduced median T2I latency from 14.90 to 3.00 seconds for Base and 2.73 to 1.08 seconds for distilled. Denoising speedups were larger, at 6.01x for Base and 4.44x for distilled Klein, but roughly half of eight-GPU distilled generation time remained outside denoising, limiting end-to-end gains.

signals.title: Tencent made the draft model guess farther. Benchmark the whole serving stack | The Plain Signal
signals.excerpt:
Tencent released a two-billion-parameter DSpine draft model for Qwen3.8-27B. Its selected tests show longer accepted drafts and higher throughput, but the useful number is not a headline multiplier. It is the gain your target model, draft, hardware, runtime and traffic shape can reproduce together.

...

A draft model is the eager junior colleague of language-model serving. It guesses the next several tokens while the larger target model checks the work. When the guesses line up, the system accepts a longer stretch in one verification cycle. When they do not, the target model corrects the sequence and the drafter tries again. The idea is called speculative decoding. The promise is more output without replacing the model users actually asked for. Tencent has now released a DSpine draft checkpoint built for Qwen3.8-27B. The checkpoint is a five-layer model with about two billion parameters, a draft block of 16 tokens and an 8,192-token sliding window. Its weights are on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0, and Tencent's public DSpine repository contains the serving integration. DSpine's architectural trick is to keep drafting positions parallel while passing a predicted predecessor feature to the next position at every layer. That gives later guesses some causal information earlier in the network instead of waiting until the backbone has finished. The new model card reports longer accepted drafts than the official DFlash2 comparison across five general benchmarks and five agent benchmark families in the configurations shown. It also reports end-to-end output throughput for recorded agent conversations replayed through SGLang. In those selected agent tests, DSpine produced 2.71 to 3.84 times the autoregressive throughput under the low reasoning setting and 2.87 to 3.55 times under xhigh reasoning. The highest reported multiplier was 3.84 times on WorkBuddy Office at low reasoning. On SWE-bench Pro replay at xhigh, the card reports about 791 output tokens per second for DSpine, about 3.19 times the autoregressive baseline and above the listed DFlash2 result of about 712. Those are project-authored numbers from one declared setup. They are not a universal coupon for 3.84 times faster AI. The card used SGLang 0.5.22, BF16 precision, FlashAttention 3 and concurrency eight. DSpine proposed blocks of 16 tokens while the DFlash2 comparison proposed eight. General tests used xhigh reasoning and at most 4,096 new tokens. Agent tests replayed 20 recorded conversations per subset, used prefix caching and allowed up to 32,768 new tokens per request. Change the GPU, runtime version, attention backend, quantization, batch shape, concurrency, prompt distribution, output length, sampling settings, cache policy or tool loop, and the result can move. This is why speculative decoding should be benchmarked as a serving stack, not admired as a model card. Keep the exact target and draft revisions. Pin SGLang and its kernels. Record precision and memory settings. Measure draft acceptance as a distribution rather than one average. Separate time to first token from inter-token latency. Report median and tail latency beside throughput. Test short chats, long reasoning, code, tool use and the traffic mix people actually send. Then check answers. The target model verifies proposed tokens, which is the core safety valve in speculative decoding. A production test should still compare outputs or sampled distributions against the non-speculative baseline. Runtime bugs, parser changes, cache behavior and sampling configuration can break the comforting theory somewhere between the paper and the endpoint. Also count the cost of the helper. The draft model consumes memory and compute. A throughput win may still be a poor trade if it reduces batch capacity, increases operational complexity or helps only the longest outputs. Tencent's release is useful because it gives Qwen3.8-27B operators a concrete open checkpoint and code path to test. The paper behind DSpine was first posted September 28 and revised October 10. The new development on November 7 is the Qwen3.8-27B draft checkpoint and serving recipe. So, yes, let the small model guess farther. Just make the whole stack show its work.

...

Tencent released a DSpine checkpoint specifically for Qwen3.8-27B. The Hugging Face model card describes a five-layer draft model with roughly two billion parameters, BF16 weights, a 16-token draft block and an 8,192-token sliding window. The target remains Qwen3.8-27B. The draft is not a standalone replacement for it. The checkpoint is licensed under Apache 2.0. The model card says no inference provider currently deploys this draft model, so operators need a compatible local or hosted serving stack of their own.

...

Tencent also published end-to-end throughput from recorded ... The card defines throughput as total output tokens divided by concurrent replay wall time. ... These are output-throughput measurements for replayed conversations, not claims about complete user-perceived latency, tool execution time or production capacity under arbitrary traffic.

...

The Qwen3.8-27B DSpine model card, repository and paper are project-authored materials. The new checkpoint results have not yet been independently reproduced in the sources reviewed for this article. The model card reports SGLang 0.5.22, BF16, FlashAttention 3 and concurrency eight. It does not present one universal hardware-neutral speedup. GPU type, memory bandwidth, driver, kernels, batching and scheduler behavior can materially change throughput and latency. DSpine and DFlash2 use different listed draft block sizes in the new comparison: 16 and eight. Acceptance length and throughput remain useful observed outcomes, but the systems are not identical except for the drafting method. Operators should compare configurations that fit their own latency and memory goals. The agent tests replay 20 conversations per subset with recorded tool-decision prefixes, prefix caching and up to 32,768 new tokens per request. Replay improves repeatability. It does not reproduce live tool latency, changing external state, user pauses, failures or every scheduler interaction in a production service. The paper's peer comparison focuses on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B and was posted before the Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. Do not transfer every paper figure to the 27B model. Use the new model card for the new checkpoint and treat both sets of results as author-reported. The draft model has about two billion parameters and needs memory and compute beside the 27B target. A server that is already memory-bound may lose batch capacity or require a different placement. Cost per useful request matters more than tokens per second in isolation. Speculative decoding should preserve the target model's result under its stated algorithm, but implementation details still need testing. Numerical precision, sampling backends, parsers, cache logic and bugs can change observable output or tool behavior. Finally, the published usage command includes trust-remote-code. Review pinned code and dependencies before production use. An open license makes inspection possible. It does not perform the inspection for you.

signals.title: AWS Web Answer turns live web research into a cited AgentCore tool - CodeGangsta
signals.excerpt:
AWS is turning web research into a managed tool that an AI agent can call once and receive a finished, cited answer. In a November 5 announcement, AWS said Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is generally available. The service is designed to replace the custom chain many agent builders assemble themselves: search, retrieve pages, judge evidence, synthesize an answer and attach citations.

The appeal is obvious, but the product is more consequential than another search API. AWS says Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, reads key pages to check facts and decides when it has enough evidence to answer. It then returns a synthesized response with citations that map claims back to source URLs. The agent builder gets a research result rather than a pile of ranked links.

...

Web Answer builds on Web Search on AgentCore, which AWS launched in June. The dividing line is control. Web Search returns URLs, titles, snippets and metadata; the developer supplies the model and owns the synthesis. Web Answer moves that synthesis into a managed tool. AWS’s technical walkthrough says the tool is intended for agents that need current web information without maintaining every step of the pipeline themselves.

...

AWS says Web Answer can be attached as a target on an AgentCore Gateway and called over the Model Context Protocol. Access is authenticated with AWS Identity and Access Management, and AWS says the managed tool operates with zero data egress. The gateway model gives administrators a central place to control which agents can invoke the capability and which permissions they carry.

...

Those controls matter because “current web information” is not a single quality level. A financial research agent, a security triage agent and a general-purpose assistant should not necessarily search the same universe of sites.

# SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints

by Shantanu Tripathi, Apoorva Chandra, and Dmitry Soldatkin on 06 NOV 2026 in Amazon SageMaker AI, Announcements, Intermediate (200) Permalink Share

When you deploy a model to a GPU endpoint, the smallest unit of GPU you can request is one whole accelerator.

...

Today, Amazon SageMaker Inference supports GPU partitioning, which uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) to divide a physical GPU into independent partitions. Each partition receives a fixed share of the GPU’s compute units and a dedicated block of its memory, with isolation enforced in hardware. That changes both constraints: you can place a different model in each partition, and you can choose a fraction of a newer accelerator instead of a whole one of either generation.

This post covers both. The first part is the direct benefit: deploy more models than you have GPUs, with isolation between them. The second is the one customers ask about when the question turns to cost: how the granularity of partitioning helps you pick the right-sized unit, and what we measured when we did.

...

## Why MIG

NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) splits one GPU into as many as seven instances, depending on the GPU. Each instance has its own compute, cache, memory and memory bandwidth. Because the split is in hardware rather than software, you get guarantees that other sharing methods can’t give:

1. Predictable latency – Each partition has dedicated memory bandwidth, so one model’s traffic spike doesn’t show up in another model’s p99.
2. Fault isolation – A crash or memory error stays inside its partition instead of taking down every model on the GPU.
3. Right-sized capacity – Small and mid-sized models get a slice that fits them instead of a whole GPU. You can mix slice sizes on one device.
4. No cold starts – Every model keeps its own partition and stays loaded, with no load penalty and no eviction.
5. Tenant isolation – Memory protection between partitions is enforced in hardware, which makes security and compliance reviews simpler.
6. Reliable planning and chargeback – A partition performs the same way regardless of its neighbors, so load tests predict production. GPU cost also maps cleanly to a model, team or tenant.

...

Four things stand out.

- The partition is faster everywhere – It delivered more output tokens per second in every scenario at every concurrency, by 53 percent to 89 percent at the load where each scenario’s cost benefit is largest, and lower inter-token latency in every one too, by 8.9 percent to 42.1 percent. The gap widens with load.
- Time to first token is lower in every case, by 5.6 percent to 47.5 percent.
- On cost it’s 18–34 percent cheaper per million output tokens, above a crossover that moves earlier as prompts lengthen. Concurrency 64 for 100-token prompts, 4 for 8,000-token prompts. Below the crossover the whole A100 is the cheaper unit. These prices are all on-demand, which at the time of analysis were measured as $25.251286 per hour for an `ml.p4d.24xlarge` and $63.296000 per hour for an `ml.p5.48xlarge` in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region. Purely for our own analysis, we derived the unit cost by dividing the whole-instance cost by the number of units on it: 8 on the p4d, and 16 on the p5, where our partition is half of a GPU.
- At the top of the ladder on long-context traffic, the A100 stopped serving. On both the 6,000- and 8,000-token workloads it failed a third to a half of its requests against a serving-path deadline, while the partition failed none. That is why those two panels end earlier than the rest.

signals.title: NVIDIA Reshard Cuts DeepSeek-V3 Weight Refit to 2.6 Seconds | TokenPost
signals.excerpt:
NVIDIA's internal benchmarks also recorded a drop from 6.1 seconds to 2.3 seconds on DGX GB200 systems.

...

Published Nov 8, 2026, 2:47 PM EST

Two GPU trays connected by a short bundle of fiber cables / TokenPost.ai

NVIDIA's Reshard collective reduced DeepSeek-V3 weight-refit time to 2.6 seconds on DGX H100 in the company's internal tests, addressing delays as reinforcement-learning systems pass updated models to inference GPUs. The conventional process took 14.9 seconds for the 671-billion-parameter model.

Weight refit moves updated model weights from the GPUs used for training to those used for inference. The inference system then uses the updated model to generate fresh training trajectories. This handoff is part of reinforcement-learning workflows, where models are trained using feedback from their outputs.

...

NVIDIA's internal benchmarks also measured the 671-billion-parameter DeepSeek-V3 model on DGX GB200 systems. Conventional refit took 6.1 seconds there, compared with 2.3 seconds using Reshard. Across tests on DGX H100 and DGX GB200 systems, the reported speedups ranged from 2.7 to 5.7 times over conventional refit.

In a separate test on a 256-GPU NVL72 cluster with NDR InfiniBand, weight-synchronization time fell from 5.78 seconds to 2.77 seconds, while the full reinforcement-learning step was 12.7% shorter. A transfer for one feed-forward mixture-of-experts layer took 9.8 milliseconds, compared with 77.3 milliseconds using flat direct sends. NVIDIA has made an open-source implementation available through its NCCL extensions repository.

signals.title: Snowflake’s ontology test favors fewer agent tools—but the benchmark is deliberately narrow — nl2sql.ai
signals.excerpt:
A two-tool GraphRAG design outscored a seven-tool knowledge-graph agent in Snowflake’s controlled biomedical test. The useful lesson is architectural, not a general leaderboard claim.

...

Snowflake has published a useful counterexample to the idea that a more capable data agent necessarily needs more tools. In a controlled biomedical evaluation, its two-tool GraphRAG configuration scored 70.0% success, while a seven-tool knowledge-graph configuration scored 60.0%. A semantic-view baseline scored 50.0%, and GraphRAG augmented with curated terminology mappings reached 78.2%.[^1]

...

Snowflake’s GraphRAG design moved more work into preprocessing. It flattened each ontology concept into a searchable profile containing names, definitions, synonyms, neighborhood information and attributes aggregated from descendants. At runtime, the agent used one search tool and one Cortex Analyst SQL tool. Snowflake says this reduced the decision surface and produced lower run-to-run variance than the other tested configurations.[^1]

...

The best score did not come from GraphRAG alone. Snowflake added eight hand-curated cell-type-to-tissue mappings and definitions for composite terms to the agent instructions. That lifted success from 70.0% to 78.2%, but Snowflake also identifies the trade-off: the mappings are static, manually maintained and only cover concepts anticipated by the designers.[^1]

...

Keep the relational semantic view as the governed SQL surface; precompute broad ontology context where retrieval can replace repeated traversal; reserve a small, reviewed mapping layer for domain phrases that hierarchy and synonym search cannot resolve.

...

Snowflake explicitly calls the evidence directional. The test uses one simplified biomedical problem, one ontology, 22 questions and vendor-tuned prompts and tool descriptions. It does not test multiple ontologies, provenance and uncertainty across mappings, workload drift,

# ExpertCrowd and HUD Collaborate to Advance AI Training and Evaluation, Release SWE Benchmark

 Toptal 

Nov 06, 2026, 10:00 ET

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ExpertCrowd, Toptal's platform for training and improving AI models and systems, today announced a collaboration with HUD, a Y Combinator-backed startup that provides tools for building AI training data through its DataVendor™ marketplace. Together, the teams released ExpertCrowd-SWE, a software engineering benchmark that evaluates the performance of frontier-grade LLMs and coding agents.

As AI systems take on increasingly complex work, measuring their capabilities requires tasks that reflect professional practice and grading criteria that capture what successful execution actually means. This collaboration brings together ExpertCrowd's expert-led task development and HUD's infrastructure for running complex RL environments.

ExpertCrowd and HUD co-developed ExpertCrowd-SWE, bringing together engineers from Toptal's global network of highly skilled domain experts with HUD's experience collaborating with frontier research teams. After Toptal's experts authored tasks and grading rubrics, HUD's infrastructure hosted task-run environments and verified the benchmarks against internal quality assurance pipelines. HUD and Toptal's AI research teams, composed of more than a dozen PhDs and researchers with educational or professional experience at Harvard, EPFL, the University of Liège, DeepMind, Qwen, and ByteDance, reviewed and assessed the methodology and results to build one of the most robust software engineering benchmarks in the industry.

...

ExpertCrowd-SWE is the first release of an ongoing Toptal-HUD collaboration, with additional initiatives in development and further announcements coming soon. Building on this foundation, ExpertCrowd and HUD will bring more specialized human expertise into the tasks, environments, and evaluations that support the next generation of AI.

signals.title: Zero Mismatch, Simple Async RL: REINFORCE Zero, DeepSeek-V4.1 and Kimi K3.1 | vLLM Blog
signals.excerpt:
TL;DR

- Asynchronous RL is faster, but it trains on samples generated by older weights.
- The rollout-to-learner gap has two parts. Weight lag changes smoothly and unclipped importance sampling (IS) controls it. Kernel mismatch, where rollout and training compute different numbers for the same weights, fluctuates and persists despite IS.
- Align the kernels, and unclipped IS corrects the remaining weight lag without sample-rejection gates. REINFORCE Zero (NVIDIA Research and Inferact) trains stably for 20,000 updates, learns at policy lag 64, and reaches 2.40× the training-step throughput of synchronous training with aligned kernels.
- Zero mismatch now covers DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (DAPO rollout step within 10% of the fast baseline), Kimi K3.1 on day 0, and both DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3.1 on AMD MI355X.
- Everything is in Inferact/zero-mismatch-rl.

...

| Setting | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Throughput, 16 GPUs, 12K updates | 2.40× the training-step throughput of synchronous training with aligned kernels (68.55 vs 164.77 hours), comparable quality |
| 20K-update reasoning, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B | Stable at lag 2 and 8; rollout-to-learner KL stays flat |
| High lag, Qwen3-4B + Python tools | Learns at lag 64 through 5,000 updates; mean reward 0.287 → about 0.78 |

| Computer use, Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni-30B on OSWorld | Pass@1 50.97% → 56.16% after 428 updates |

signals.title: Zyphra introduces ZYFA : FlashAttention FP8 for AMD MI355X, up to 1.76x faster
signals.excerpt:
Zyphra has released ZYFA (Zyphra FlashAttention on AMD), a set of FP8 and BF16 attention compute kernels designed for AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs. According to the company, its FP8 kernels are between 1.16 and 1.76 times faster than AITER, AMD’s default kernel library, on real model activations. The code is released as open source under the Apache 2.0 license.

- Zyphra released ZYFA, an open-source set of FP8 and BF16 attention kernels for AMD MI355X GPUs.
- Its FP8 kernels run 1.16 to 1.76 times faster than AMD’s AITER on real model activations.
- Lean P, ping-pong scheduling and block scaling overlap softmax work with matrix work to close the bottleneck.
- ZYFA handles only causal forward-pass prefill and works only on MI355X.

ZYFA is an FP8 attention engine designed for the prefill phase, i.e., processing the provided context before generating the response, on long contexts. It powers the Zyphra Optimization Engine (ZOE), which runs Zyphra Cloud. The BF16 kernels are written in HIP, while the FP8 kernels are hand-scheduled assembly code, produced by a generator written in Python.

...

On real activations at 16K, FP8 gains reach 1.16x for Mistral-7B, 1.17x for Qwen3-8B, and 1.76x for DeepSeek-V2-Lite. On Gaussian benchmarks at 32K, the FP8 kernel with head dimension 128 achieves 2,672 TFLOP/s, compared to 1,944 for AITER. The kernel also leads on the MLA form, with 2,464 TFLOP/s versus 1,237, a ratio of 1.99.

...

Compared to an fp64 calculation, ZYFA’s FP8 error is 0.22 times that of AITER on Mistral-7B and 0.38 times on Qwen3-8B. On the full Mistral-7B model, the KL divergence, which measures the difference between two probability distributions, reaches 3.4×10⁻³ with ZYFA and 5.9×10⁻³ with AITER. Zyphra also notes that ZYFA is limited to causal forward-pass prefill, without decoding or paged KV cache, and that it only works on MI355X.

signals.title: Mistral Launches Managed Agents and Vector Search: Why Enterprise AI Discovery Is Moving Beyond Public Search
signals.excerpt:
November 6, 2026. France-based Mistral AI has released a coordinated set of platform features designed to help developers build, deploy, connect and evaluate AI agents. Announced in the company's November 5 release notes, the updates include Managed Agents, Managed Search Index, HTTP API Connectors and a natural-language Workflow Builder.

...

Availability matters. Managed Agents, Managed Search Index and Workflow Builder are in public preview, while HTTP API Connectors are in private preview. These are confirmed product releases, but not a declaration that every feature is generally available to every Mistral account.

## Four updates, one enterprise-agent architecture

| Capability | What it does | Availability on Nov. 5 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Managed Agents | Runs durable Python agents with background execution, resumable sessions and approval gates | Public preview |
| Managed Search Index | Hosts a vector index for ingesting and retrieving enterprise data | Public preview |
| HTTP API Connectors | Connects agents and workflows to described HTTP APIs without requiring an MCP server | Private preview |
| Workflow Builder | Turns a natural-language description into inspectable, testable and deployable workflow code | Public preview |

...

## Managed Agents: long-running tasks that survive interruptions

Managed Agents is built around Mistral's Python Agents SDK, `mistralai-agents`. Developers define models, instructions, tools and environment once, then run the same agent in their own process, self-host it with `agents serve` or deploy it on Mistral's infrastructure with `agents deploy`. The `agents init` command scaffolds a starter project.

The defining feature is durable execution. Mistral says deployed agents can work for hours or days in the background and resume from the last completed step after a crash or interruption. Sessions are stored by Mistral, reducing the need for developers to operate a separate session database. The platform supports human approval for selected tool calls, live steering, interruption and later resumption.

...

## Managed Search Index: retrieval without operating a vector database

Mistral's Managed Search Index lets developers provision a hosted vector index by specifying a name, an embedding model and optionally a schema. They can ingest and query enterprise information through the SDK, using the same Search Toolkit ingestion pipelines, QueryEngine and retrievers supported by other backends. Mistral operates the underlying storage.

This is an infrastructure release, not a new consumer search engine. A vector index supports semantic retrieval: information can be found based on meaning rather than only exact keyword matches. An agent can use retrieved documents as grounding for an answer, reducing the need to rely solely on the model's internal knowledge.

However, a vector index does not automatically ensure factual accuracy. A well-written answer can still be grounded in the wrong document, an outdated version or content the user should not have permission to access. A production implementation needs access controls, document versioning, source attribution, relevance evaluation and a policy for what happens when retrieval confidence is low.

...

## Why RAG architecture matters more than the model brand

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) combines search with generation. A typical workflow ingests documents, chunks them into retrievable units, creates embeddings, retrieves relevant passages and supplies those passages to a language model. The quality of the final answer depends on each stage.

A managed index reduces operational complexity but does not solve poor document structure, ambiguous identifiers or inconsistent metadata. A product catalog with missing SKUs, outdated availability and duplicate descriptions can still produce misleading answers. In fact, retrieval quality becomes more important when an agent can take action on the result.

signals.excerpt:
Perplexity has reworked every effort level of its Agent API, the managed research runtime that developers call with a single effort parameter instead of wiring together a model, a search tool and a step budget themselves. In a post dated November 5, 2026, the company says each level now costs less per query while research quality is higher or unchanged, and it introduces a sixth level, ultra, for the broadest research jobs. The headline figure belongs to medium: its accuracy on the public BrowseComp and DSQA research benchmarks rose from 55% to 77% while its cost per query fell by almost 90%, according to Perplexity.

...

Applications that request a level by name receive the new configurations automatically, without code changes. Teams that need stable behavior can pin a date-stamped version of a level, such as fast@2026-10-16.0, and the first ultra release carries the stamp ultra@2026-11-05.0 in the developer changelog. Perplexity attributes the savings to how each level spends steps, tokens and tool calls, and to cheaper search options such as Fast Search.

...

The effort parameter selects a bundle of settings maintained by Perplexity: the backing model, the number of agent steps, the reasoning setting passed to that model, the output ceiling and the tools the agent may call. It is a separate control from reasoning.effort, which only sets how hard the selected model thinks inside each step. The current configurations, as published in the Agent API documentation on November 7, 2026, look as follows.

signals.title: Google Open-Sources the Engine Behind Its Biggest Products - GEroundtable
signals.excerpt:
On 5 November, Google open-sourced the inference engine that already answers more than six million queries every second inside its own products. XLA Serving Engine, a C++ runtime for the OpenXLA ecosystem, moves machine-learning models out of Python and into production serving, and Google says it powers YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, Search and parts of Gemini Omni. The release turns a year of internal production use into public infrastructure anyone can now run.

...

Most machine-learning engineers train models in Python, using frameworks such as JAX and PyTorch, but many production environments refuse Python because of its deployment and operational complexity. XLA Serving Engine bridges that gap with what Google calls a “Train in Python, Serve in C++” workflow, exporting a model into a compiled format that a native C++ runtime can execute directly.

The export format is an XLA SavedModel, which stores the model’s computation as StableHLO, a portable intermediate representation, while Orbax checkpointing stores the weights. Once exported, the XLA Serving Runtime loads the artifact, wraps the PJRT execution interface directly, and applies the XLA compiler’s optimisations, cutting out the Python interpreter and its global interpreter lock entirely.

...

For short requests, Google reports that the engine delivers two to five times the throughput of the best Python server its team could build, and eight to thirty-six times that of a straightforward one. It uses thirty to seventy percent less CPU time per prediction and roughly a quarter of the memory, though these are Google’s measurements and remain unverified.

...

Google is candid about the engine’s limits. It is a lightweight, one-shot inference engine, and for large autoregressive language models with long context lengths, the company recommends established projects such as vLLM or SGLang, which handle LLM-specific memory management. The engine is aimed at vision, embedding and recommendation models rather than chatbots.

Google plans TorchTPU integration so PyTorch users can export models to the same format and serve them on TPUs in C++, plus ahead-of-time compilation to cut cold-start times and a C++ data preprocessor for teams wanting preprocessing inside the model graph. Docker images tested on CPU, GPU and TPU, with simple gRPC APIs, are available now.
